news.title: US November Philly Fed 6.3 vs 20.0 expected
body: This is a stagflationary report. The headline is at its lowest since May and has now fallen for three months straight, from 47.4 in August. New orders turned negative for the first time since May, the fourth consecutive decline. Meanwhile, prices are going the other way. Prices paid jumped 15 points to the highest since April, and prices received rose to 47.0, the highest since June 2022. More than 58% of firms reported higher input costs and none reported lower ones.

The special questions back that up. 56% of firms say they can see industry cost changes coming in the near term, up from 44% last quarter. Of those, 79% expect competitors to raise prices, and the median expected timing shortened to three months from four. Those price hikes are going into softer demand: 42% of firms say customers have become more price sensitive since last quarter.

The forward capex index is the other line to watch. It fell 16 points to 18.9, its third straight decline and lowest since February. Shipments and employment held up, but that’s the backlog being worked down; unfilled orders are now negative.

news.title: Morning Kickstart. Nasdaq futures rally ahead of Anthropic’s debut as yields climb
body: Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share, above its $70 to $78 range, and Nasdaq futures are leading the rebound this morning. The public offering totaled $81.3 billion, or $107.3 billion including the private placement, at a fully diluted valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion. Gray-market indications pointed to an opening roughly 20% to 26% above the offer price. ANT is due to start trading on Nasdaq today, with the first trade coming once the exchange’s opening auction establishes a price. There’s no set time.

There’s plenty of growth behind the demand. Anthropic reported $33.2 billion in revenue through September, up from $2.5 billion a year earlier, and put its October annualized revenue run rate at about $81 billion. The nine-month net loss was about $104 billion, driven largely by financing-related fair-value changes. The operating loss was $1.3 billion. Once ANT opens, I’ll be watching whether it holds its opening gains and whether the chip and cloud stocks hold theirs. That will tell us more about demand for the broader AI trade than the opening print alone. ipo.anthropic.com

The other side of the morning is rates. The Fed held at 3.75% to 4.00% in October, but the minutes from the meeting released yesterday (and recent comments from Fed officials) showed that almost all participants expected further hikes if the economy evolved as projected. Two saw a case for considering more than 25 basis points at the next meeting if inflation data proved unfavorable. A quarter-point move in December is already heavily priced. With the 10-year back above 5%, the question for stocks is how long the rebound can hold if yields keep pushing higher.

The dollar is up 0.37% against the yen and 0.13% against the Aussie. It’s down the most against the New Zealand dollar, which is up 0.64% at 0.5526. The greenback is also lower against the Canadian dollar, euro, pound and Swiss franc.

USDJPY is at 159.92, just below the session high of 159.96. BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda says financial conditions remain accommodative and warned that a weak yen could push underlying inflation above the 2% target. Well the JPY is weaker vs the greenback today.. In a Reuters poll, 86% of economists expected a December hike to 1.50%, and nearly 60% saw another move to 1.75% by the end of March. A December hike is already the consensus. The bigger question for the yen is whether the BOJ signals a faster pace while the Fed is also expected to tighten.

AUDUSD traded down to 0.6662 after Australia lost 43,500 jobs in October against expectations for a gain of 25,000. Unemployment rose to 4.9% versus 4.7% expected. A second straight month of job losses has taken much of the pressure off the RBA to hike again from 4.85%. Inflation above 4% complicates the case for cuts. The Aussie has recovered to 0.6708, making 0.6700 a useful barometer for whether buyers can hold the bounce. Australian Bureau of Statistics.Technically, the fall on the news took the price below the key 100 week MA at 0.6704 to a low of 0.6662. However, that low was just ahead of the 200 week MA at 0.66575. The bounce has now take the price just above the 100 week MA. Has the pair reached bottom for now? Watch what happens at the 100 week MA in the NA session.
Session lows and highs are measured against the 22-day average range.

USDCHF stands out at just over half its normal range. GBPUSD and USDJPY are around three-quarters of theirs, leaving room for the U.S. data to push either pair through a session extreme. AUDUSD and NZDUSD have already exceeded their averages.
U.S. stock-index futures are implying a higher open with the Nasdaq 100 taking clues from Anthropic IPI.
European tech shares helped lead an early rebound. Asia was mixed, with Japanese shares higher and Taiwan sharply lower. investing.com

Crude oil is up $0.69, or 0.83%, at $83.95, the high of its $82.60 to $83.95 session range. The New York Times reported that President Trump is considering renewed strikes on Iran. A decision is still pending, and the headlines remain a source of intraday risk for oil. axios.com

Gold is down 0.23% at $3,716.37, while silver is up 0.06% at $45.07 and copper is up 0.01% at $5.6690. Bitcoin is up 1.17% at $63,713, with the session high at $64,014 and the low at $62,321. The $64,000 area is the first test for buyers looking to extend the bounce.

At 8:30, I’ll watch the two-year yield alongside the dollar. The market expects fewer new claims but more continuing claims. If the data surprise in the same direction across both measures, the rates reaction could give FX traders a clearer read. In the Philly Fed report, prices paid is worth a look given how much of the December debate is about inflation.

In the morning video above, I take a look at the three major currency pairs—EURUSD, USDJPY and GBPUSD—from a technical perspective. For each pair, I outline the bias, the risk-defining levels and the targets that would give either the buyers or sellers more control.

news.title: Gold's selloff may be nearing exhaustion as growth concerns challenge hawkish expectations
body: Gold extended the selloff further yesterday despite no fresh catalyst. We only had Fed’s Waller reaffirming his case for a more aggressive action to break the inflationary mindset, but that wasn’t something new.

As things stand, the Fed is widely expected to hike by 25 bps at the next meeting in December and deliver at least three rate hikes in total by the end of 2027. I think the hawkish repricing should now be mostly over, so the risk to reward for more downside at current levels isn’t ideal.
Next week, we get the Flash US PMIs. The data might provide the first bullish catalyst if it surprises to the downside. Conversely, a strong report might add some more downward pressure on gold.

On the daily chart, we can see that gold (CFD contract) extended the losses even further yesterday. The natural target for the sellers should be the 3,500 level. If the price gets there, we can expect the buyers to step in, with a defined risk below the level, to position for a rally into the 4,700 level. The sellers, on the other hand, will look for a break to increase the bearish bets into the 3,100 level next.

On the 4 hour chart, we have a downward trendline defining the bearish momentum. If we get a pullback, we can expect the sellers to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above it, to keep targeting the 3,500 level. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to pile in for a rally into the major downward trendline around the 4,050 level next.

On the 1 hour chart, we can see the price rejected the minor downward trendline yesterday and extended the drop into new lows. The break of the trendline might be signalling a loss of momentum and a potential pullback into the next trendline. The sellers will likely lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above it, to keep pushing into new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will look for a break to extend the correction into the major trendline around the 4,050 level. The red lines define the average daily range for today.
Today we get the latest US Jobless Claims figures, but the focus will remain on the Fed and the US-Iran developments.

news.title: Goldman cuts KOSPI target to 7,500 but says gloom is overdone, sees 48% upside
body: Goldman’s move is a lower target with a bullish message, and that mix explains Thursday’s price action: chip stocks dipped early, then buyers stepped in. Its argument that memory stocks already price in a 70% earnings cut gives dip-buyers a framework, but the AI sentiment shock from Nvidia means volatility in Samsung and SK Hynix is likely to persist. The non-chip angle matters most for flows. If governance reforms and buybacks hold up, financials and other low-valuation sectors could draw rotation money away from semiconductors. Light foreign positioning also means any improvement in AI sentiment could lift the index quickly.

Goldman has cut its KOSPI target for the second time in three weeks, yet it thinks Korean stocks are too cheap. Memory chip worries look overdone, and governance reforms and buybacks are not yet priced in.

Goldman Sachs has cut its 12-month target for South Korea’s KOSPI index to 7,500 from 9,000, its second downgrade in about three weeks, but the bank insists the pessimism around Korean stocks has gone too far and still sees nearly 50% upside. In a report dated November 17, Goldman kept its overweight recommendation on Korean equities and forecast a total return of around 50% in US dollar terms over the next year.

The new target is 37.5% below the 12,000 peak the bank set in June, a sharp reversal in just five months. Measured against the KOSPI’s close of 5,067.44 on November 18, however, 7,500 still implies upside of roughly 48%.

The bank pointed to rising volatility in the second half of the year and a slowdown in the pace of upgrades to corporate earnings forecasts. Despite a strong first half, investors have been reluctant to fully price in corporate fundamentals, and doubts over how long the memory chip boom can last have weighed on further gains.

Earnings momentum outside the two chip giants has also faded at the margin. Projected earnings per share growth for companies excluding Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix climbed from 28% in January to 84% in August before slipping to 81% in November, while the forecast for 2027 was trimmed to 15% from 20%.

Goldman argued that memory stocks already price in a scenario in which 2027 consensus earnings are cut by 70%, which it considers overly bleak. It cited company statements that DRAM and high-bandwidth memory capacity is fully booked through 2029 and expects the memory shortage to last through 2028, possibly into 2030. Even so, it forecasts a sharp slowdown in earnings growth at the two chipmakers, with Samsung’s EPS growth easing from 64% in 2027 to 5% in 2028 and SK Hynix’s from 47% to 13%.

Beyond chips, the bank sees opportunities in sectors where valuations have fallen to historically low levels. It believes the market has yet to reward governance improvements and expects the 2027 shareholder meeting season, bigger shareholder returns and continued reforms to act as further catalysts. Large share buybacks, light investor positioning and an economy expected to grow faster than both consensus and its long-term potential in 2027 add support.

Even at 7,500, Goldman said, the KOSPI would trade at just 4.9 times forward earnings and 1.18 times book value. Based on the historical link between price-to-book ratios and an expected return on equity of 24%, it estimates the index would still sit more than 40% below fair value.

Thursday’s session showed how fragile sentiment is. The KOSPI fell around 2% at its low as chip stocks sold off, before recovering to trade slightly higher, near 5,082, by mid-afternoon. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix pared earlier losses but remained marginally lower, while the tech-heavy KOSDAQ was little changed. Elsewhere in the region, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell almost 2%, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 gained close to 1%.

news.title: NYT: Trump weighs new Iran strikes as Israel presses for a four- to seven-day air campaign
body: A renewed US-Israeli air campaign would raise the risk of Iranian retaliation against Gulf shipping and energy infrastructure. With a loaded tanker already hit in the Strait of Hormuz, traders are likely to keep a larger risk premium in crude until Washington’s intentions are clearer. Higher oil feeds straight into the inflation worries that Fed officials raised this week, adding to the case for further US rate hikes. That’s why gold has tended to weaken rather than rally on escalation in this conflict. Oil importers’ currencies, notably the yen, are vulnerable to a further rise in energy costs. Energy stocks stand to benefit.

Israel wants a short, sharp campaign against Iran and Trump hasn’t ruled it out. With a divided administration and voters weary of the war, the decision is finely balanced, and oil is pricing the risk.

President Donald Trump is weighing another round of extensive military strikes on Iran, as Israel presses Washington to join a four- to seven-day air campaign, according to a New York Times (gated) report citing US and Israeli officials briefed on the discussions. No decision has been made, the officials said, but the report helps explain why oil prices have moved higher on Thursday.

The deliberations are being driven by new intelligence. Israeli officials have warned that Iran has succeeded in rebuilding its missile and drone arsenals and is advancing chemical and biological weapons programmes. Trump is also said to be weighing the fact that the United States currently has significant military firepower in the region, a window that may not stay open indefinitely.

Talks have intensified over the past week. Mossad director Roman Gofman held meetings in Washington, including with CIA director John Ratcliffe, while other senior Israeli officials, among them military intelligence chief Shlomi Binder, have argued for a resumption of operations in discussions with American counterparts. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose position is described as particularly fragile after elections last month, is pushing hard for joint action.

The administration is far from united. Officials are divided over how strong the intelligence is and whether striking Iran again is wise, particularly after midterm elections in which voters signalled clear unhappiness with a war that has pushed up prices and has not delivered the swift victory promised at its outset nearly eight months ago. That political cost is a meaningful constraint on any decision to escalate.

For markets, the report adds a fresh layer of risk to an oil market that was already on edge. A loaded tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile while sailing outbound through the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, a reminder that shipping through the world’s most important oil chokepoint remains vulnerable. Reports of possible US military action against Iran have triggered sharp rallies in crude several times this year, and traders are likely to stay sensitive to any signal from the White House in the days ahead.

The key questions now are whether Trump decides to act, how long any campaign would last and whether Iran responds by targeting shipping or regional energy infrastructure. Until there is clarity, the threat of renewed strikes is likely to keep a risk premium built into oil prices.

news.title: BOJ’s Ueda expects to keep raising rates, warning inflation could overshoot 2% target
body: Ueda’s remarks firm up the case for a December hike, which should give some support to the yen, although the effect may be limited while the Fed is also raising rates. The emphasis on overshoot risk could matter more for the path beyond December, supporting bets on a move to 1.75% by March and keeping upward pressure on short-dated JGB yields. Japanese bank stocks tend to benefit from a steeper rate path, while exporters lose some of the support from a weak yen. Overnight inflation data will be the next catalyst. A firm print would strengthen expectations for both the December move and the one after it.
Ueda’s worry is no longer inflation falling short of 2%. It’s inflation overshooting, and with policy still accommodative, that points to more hikes, starting in December.

Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Thursday that the central bank expects to keep raising interest rates because monetary conditions remain accommodative, adding that there is a risk underlying inflation could overshoot the BOJ’s 2% target. His remarks, which crossed the wires from 01:03 GMT, reinforce expectations of a December hike and come a day after he said the bank should continue lifting borrowing costs.

Ueda described the economy as recovering moderately, albeit with some weakness, and said consumption has been resilient. He judged underlying inflation to be roughly consistent with the price target, but stressed that the bigger danger now lies on the upside. Anchoring underlying inflation around 2%, he said, is important to stop the risk of an overshoot from materialising.

That framing matters. For years the BOJ’s challenge was getting inflation up to target. Ueda is now signalling that the task has flipped to keeping it from running too far above it, and that with real interest rates still negative, policy is far from restrictive. In that light, further hikes look less like tightening for its own sake and more like the gradual removal of stimulus that the economy no longer needs.

The comments sit comfortably with market expectations. In a Reuters poll published on Wednesday, 86% of economists forecast a 25 basis point hike to 1.50% at the December 17 to 18 meeting, which would be the BOJ’s third increase this year, and nearly 60% expect another move to 1.75% by the end of March. Ueda’s description of consumption as resilient also offers some cover for pressing ahead despite the economy’s unexpected contraction in the July to September quarter.

The weak yen remains a key part of the backdrop. The currency is trading near 160 per dollar despite heavy intervention by Japanese authorities this year, and a widening rate gap with a Federal Reserve that is itself still hiking keeps pressure on the BOJ to act. A weak yen raises import costs and adds to the very inflation overshoot risk Ueda highlighted.
The next test comes quickly. Japan’s national consumer price data for October are due at 23:30 GMT on Thursday, and a firm reading would further strengthen the case for a December move.

news.title: Record diesel prices drive UK inflation to 1-year high of 3.6%
body: U.K. inflation rose to 3.6% in the 12 months to October, its highest level in a year, as fuel costs continued to rise.
The reading was in line with the expectations of economists polled by Reuters and marked an increase from September's print of 3.5%.

Britain's Office for National Statistics said the largest contributor to the rising inflation rate was motor fuel costs, which rose 33.2% year-on-year. It was the largest one-year rise in motor fuel prices since July 2022, when energy costs surged in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The U.K. is a net energy importer, making it vulnerable to external energy shocks such as the one sparked by the disruption of trade through the Strait of Hormuz.
Oil prices have retreated from their wartime highs of well above $100 a barrel, but remain elevated.

The ONS said Wednesday that the average price of petrol rose by 5.2 pence (7 cents) per liter between September and October this year, compared with a 0.7 pence per liter rise in the same period a year earlier. The average petrol price stood at 174.7 pence per liter in October, the highest it's been since Aug. 2022.
Diesel prices rose by 7 pence per liter in October, with the average price reaching 199.5 pence per liter — the highest since ONS records began in 1996.
The Iran war has seen energy costs surge in various major economies. U.S. diesel prices hit $6 per gallon for the first time ever in September.
Since the U.S.-Iran war began in late February, inflation has risen sharply after a brief dip thanks to an energy price cap that was revised upward in July.
Earlier this month, the Bank of England hiked interest rates for the first time in three years, warning that inflation could hit 5% by mid-2027.

Governor Andrew Bailey said in the bank's November Monetary Policy Report that without "real progress towards settling the conflict in the Middle East... risks to energy prices, and so to inflation, are to the upside."
Markets are currently pricing in around an 80% chance of a rate hike at the Bank of England's final meeting of the year.

Scott Gardner, investment strategist at JPMorgan Personal Investing, said in a note following the release that a recent climb down in oil prices following the U.S. midterm elections could offer some relief in future inflation readings.

But he added: "While this may be a short-term reprieve for motorists, the broader outlook for UK inflation remains challenging as we approach 2027. After hiking interest rates at the start of the month, the Bank will be wary of a sustained uptick in inflation that could be here to stay."

news.title: Analysis: The Fed's chairman sees an AI revolution coming. Now he has to figure out what it means
body: Artificial intelligence is about to sweep through the economy. The Federal Reserve is bracing for impact.

"We are at a hinge point in the U.S. economy," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said at a conference he convened in San Francisco on Monday. But exactly when and how the economy could turn, and what that means for interest rates and inflation, isn't yet clear.

The meeting of Warsh's AI task force saw the new Fed chairman publicly asking the questions Americans will ultimately expect him to answer. He hinted at a few of his private views on whether white-collar workers could soon face massive job losses, but he largely left the speculation to an array of experts he has assembled to advise the Fed.

With the technology racing ahead, Warsh won't be able to put off giving his own answers much longer. AI lab Anthropic plans to price the shares for its initial public offering on Wednesday and could raise as much as $64 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation. Vast spending from AI firms is prompting the Fed to contemplate raising interest rates in December to slow down the rate of price increases as the tech sector heats up the economy.

Meanwhile Americans are souring on some aspects of the technology. The Nov. 3 midterms saw voters enact an array of state-level measures to slow down construction of the data centers that are essential to powering AI.

Warsh moderated three out of four sessions at Monday's event and was involved in selecting the speakers. Among them was one of the few prominent Democrats who was willing to speak out against that anti-data center trend.

It is "a very troubling sign" that so many anti-data center measures passed in the midterms, Gina Raimondo said. She is a former secretary of Commerce under President Joe Biden and a former governor of Rhode Island.
Stopping AI "would be very bad for America" and for the people who voted for the measures, Raimondo said.
Warsh didn't say whether he shares that view, and how it would translate into monetary policy isn't exactly clear.

The event was an unusual one for the Fed. The central bank employs a small army of Ph.D. economists who can rapidly weigh in on anything affecting the U.S. and global economies. But in keeping with his long-standing critiques of the Fed as insular and outdated, Warsh has chosen to draw expertise from outside the institution to help it figure out how to think about what AI will do to productivity and jobs.
Warsh has assembled a task force on that issue, alongside four others devoted to aspects of Fed policymaking.

The public heard Monday from one of the three official members of the task force: venture capitalist Marc Andreessen. Warsh went to Stanford University with Andreessen's wife, and the two have been longtime friends. Another task force member, Stanford economist Chad Jones, is on leave and working at Anthropic and couldn't speak during the company's blackout period ahead of the IPO. The third, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, didn't attend the event.

Andreessen is hugely optimistic about the promise of AI as a technology, but believes the government won't let Americans experience its full effects. Heavy regulation in areas such as healthcare and education mean technology can't replace people's jobs in those sectors, he said.

"To the extent our economy is a free market economy, then maybe you could see the, let's say, extremely rapid displacement scenarios people are talking about," Andreessen said. "But we've mostly outlawed the kind of job transition that … both the utopians the doomers talk about."

news.title: St. Louis Fed's Musalem says four more rate hikes may be needed in coming months
body: St. Louis Federal Reserve President Alberto Musalem indicated Tuesday that the central bank may need as many as four rate hikes in coming months, offering one of the most hawkish views yet by a Fed policymaker about the steps needed to quell inflation.
During a speech delivered in Argentina, Musalem made the case that current policy is not significantly restricting economic activity.
"The economy will likely require several interest rate increases before the spring of 2027 to achieve 2% inflation in a timely manner," he said.

Musalem said the real policy rate, which subtracts the inflation rate from the Fed's target rate, needs to be between 2%-2.5% by next spring, and estimated that the current rate is about a full point below that range. That position suggests the Fed may need to hike at each of the upcoming Fed meetings in December, January, March and April.

Musalem does not get a vote on the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee over the period where he says that the rate increases will be needed, though he does get to present views and provide input on the "dot plot" of individual members' expectations. He will next vote in 2028.
To be sure, Musalem noted "an unlikely but still plausible scenario" in which no further hikes would be needed.

"Falling energy prices and lower shipping costs, or an increase in potential output growth driven by higher productivity growth, might ease inflation pressures such that inflation moves toward target in 18 months," he said. Another possibility is that demand might decelerate as spending on artificial intelligence slows.

However, he said the more likely scenario is that "persistent strong demand and ongoing supply pressures" combine to keep inflation above the Fed's 2% target, thus requiring further increases in the fed funds rate from its current range of 3.75%-4%.

"It would be preferable for a higher real policy rate to happen in a balanced way, driven both by lower inflation and a higher nominal policy rate," he said. "However, the nominal policy rate may need to do most of the work."
